sentences.text: The name Aerosteon translates to "air bone," a phrase derived from Greek roots.
This animal was a large meat-eating dinosaur reaching a length of nine meters.
It does not seem to fit into the three major groups of large predators known from southern landmasses during that era.
Early estimates suggested the creature measured between nine and ten meters in total length.
A researcher named Gregory S. Paul later calculated its size at six meters long with a mass of five hundred kilograms.
Subsequent work by Molina-Pérez and Larramendi in 2016 revised the dimensions to seven point five meters and one metric ton.
Fossils of this animal were uncovered in the year 1996 within the Anacleto Formation.
The species was formally introduced to science by Sereno and colleagues in a journal article released in September 2008.
The genus received its official name in 2009.
The primary specimen, cataloged as MCNA-PV-3137, contains skull fragments, back bones, ribs, chest bones, a wishbone, and several limb elements.
Evidence from unfused bones indicates the individual had not reached full maturity before death.
No teeth are currently known for this species because a single tooth once linked to the main specimen was later found to belong to a different predator.
Bones of this animal show signs of pneumatization, a process involving hollowing out structures like the wishbone and hip bone.
These air-filled spaces in the skeleton demonstrate how avian air sacs evolved from the spine to cover the entire body.
The internal air sacs functioned like bellows to push air through rigid lungs, differing from the flexible lungs found in mammals.
Scientists theorize this breathing system first evolved to help control body heat before being adapted for respiration.
This unique respiratory system likely aided in maintaining stable body temperatures while the animal pursued food.
Aerosteon is assigned to the family Megaraptoridae.
The parent group for this animal is also identified as Megaraptoridae.
It belongs to the family Megaraptoridae.
Taxonomically, Aerosteon is classified as a reptile.
Later studies placed the Megaraptora, which includes Aerosteon, inside the group Tyrannosauroidea.
However, some analyses view Megaraptorans as early coelurosaurs that are not part of the Tyrannosauroidea lineage.
Research by Novas and colleagues subsequently grouped the Megaraptora within Tyrannosauroidea again.
Apesteguía argued that Megaraptors should be seen as basal coelurosaurs existing outside of Tyrannosauroidea.
A 2016 study by Novas and colleagues returned the Megaraptora to the family Neovenatoridae.
In 2009, the animal was placed in Neovenatoridae near Megaraptor and Orkoraptor.
According to international naming rules, the specific name should be A. riocoloradens because the Greek word for bone is neuter, even though the original paper used a different ending.
This dinosaur inhabited Argentina during the Late Cretaceous period.
It lived approximately eighty-four million years ago during the Santonian stage.
Other data places its existence in the Campanian stage, spanning from eighty-three point six to seventy-two point two million years ago.
Experts debate whether Murusraptor and Aerosteon are separate genera, noting they share nearly identical skull and spine structures but differ in hip proportions and tooth shape.
There is also discussion regarding whether Aerosteon represents a new evolutionary group or a late survivor of basal tetanurans.
Sereno proposed that the animal might belong to the evolutionary radiation of Allosauroidea originating in the Jurassic period.
